useCases.scenario: Safely read a possibly absent position.

Negative indexes count backward from the array's end, with -1 selecting the last element.
The index is zero-based and converted to an integer before lookup.
For a negative index, the effective position is calculated by adding it to the array length.
A successful lookup returns the matching array element.
For non-negative integer indexes, at(index) gives the same element as bracket notation.
Use at() for relative reads and with() when a corresponding relative-index update is needed.

Array methods::Array.prototype.filter.summary: Builds a new shallow array containing the elements for which a predicate returns a truthy value. The original array is not changed.

JavaScript invokes the predicate for each assigned array element, passing the element, its index, and the original array; elements whose predicate result is truthy are copied into a new shallow array. The optional thisArg supplies this for the predicate.

Array methods::Array.prototype.filter.returns: A new shallow array containing the elements for which callbackFn returns a truthy value; if none pass, an empty array.

It returns a separate array containing each element whose predicate result is truthy.
Falsy predicate results exclude elements from the result.
The returned array is a shallow copy, so retained object references are not deep-cloned.
When every predicate result is falsy, filter returns an empty array.
The callback receives the current element, its index, and the array on which filter was called.

Array methods::Array.prototype.find and.summary: `find()` returns the first array element whose predicate is truthy; `findLast()` returns the last matching element. Both return `undefined` when no element matches.

findLast(callbackFn)

parameters.description: A value used as `this` when calling `callbackFn`.

Array methods::Array.prototype.find and.returns: The last (highest-index) element satisfying the predicate, or `undefined` when no element matches.

The returned value is the matching element itself, not its index.
A missing match produces `undefined`.
Use `find()` when the desired match is the earliest one in normal array order.
The method repeatedly applies a predicate while scanning the array.
The predicate is called for each visited element until a match is found.
Because it is generic, the method can operate on suitable array-like values.

Array methods::Array.prototype.flat and.summary: flat() creates a new array by recursively flattening nested arrays to a chosen depth, defaulting to one level. flatMap() maps each element and flattens the callback results by one level in the same operation.

parameters.description: Function executed for each source element. It may return an array to flatten by one level or a non-array value to append directly.

parameters.name: thisArg
parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn runs.

Array methods::Array.prototype.flat and.returns: Both methods return a new array. flat() contains elements concatenated through the requested depth; flatMap() contains callback results flattened by one level.

example.explanation: Use flat() to copy and flatten nested arrays to a chosen depth; use flatMap() when each element must first produce a value or array and the results should be flattened one level.

The optional depth controls flattening depth and defaults to 1.
flat() returns a new array rather than changing the original array.
flatMap() maps each element and then flattens the mapped results by one level.

flatMap() does not flatten non-array callback results; it appends them as single values.

Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.summary: Use includes() to test whether an array contains a value, or indexOf() to obtain the first matching index. includes() returns a boolean; indexOf() returns an index or -1.
Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.explanation: Use Array.prototype.includes() when the result should be true or false. Use Array.prototype.indexOf() when you need the first matching index; it returns -1 when no match exists.

includes(searchElement, fromIndex)
indexOf(searchElement)

parameters.name: searchElement
parameters.description: The value or element to search for.

parameters.name: fromIndex
parameters.description: Optional zero-based position from which to begin searching; converted to an integer. Negative values count from the end.

Array methods::Array.prototype.includes.returns: includes() returns true when the value is found and false otherwise. indexOf() returns the first matching index, or -1 when the value is absent.

console.log(values.includes(NaN)); // true
console.log(values.indexOf("a"));   // 0

console.log(values.includes("b", 2)); // true

Array methods::Array.prototype.join.summary: Array.prototype.join() converts an array’s elements to one string, placing a chosen separator between adjacent elements. It uses commas by default and returns an empty string for an empty array.

parameters.name: separator
parameters.description: A string placed between each adjacent pair of elements. If omitted, a comma is used.

Array methods::Array.prototype.join.returns: A string containing all array elements joined together; an empty array returns the empty string.

Array methods::Array.prototype.map.summary: Creates a new array by applying a callback to every present element of an array. Each callback result becomes the corresponding element in the new array.

parameters.name: callbackFn

parameters.description: Optional value used as this when callbackFn executes.

Array methods::Array.prototype.reduce.summary: Array.prototype.reduce() runs a callback from left to right, carrying each callback result into the next call. It returns the final accumulated value, optionally starting from an explicitly supplied initial value.

Array methods::Array.prototype.slice and.summary: Use `slice()` to copy a range into a new shallow array without mutation. Use `splice()` to remove, replace, or insert elements in the existing array and receive the deleted elements.
Array methods::Array.prototype.slice and.explanation: Use `slice(start, end)` to create a shallow copy of the range from `start` through just before `end`; it leaves the source unchanged. Use `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` to mutate the source by deleting elements and inserting supplied items at the same position; it returns the deleted elements.

slice()
slice(start)
slice(start, end)

splice(start)

splice(start, deleteCount, item1, item2)
splice(start, deleteCount, item1, item2, /* …, */ itemN)

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Zero-based index at which to start extraction, converted to an integer. Negative values count from the end; omitted `start` defaults to 0.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: Zero-based index at which to end extraction, converted to an integer; extraction stops before this index. If omitted, extraction continues to the end.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Zero-based index at which to start changing the array, converted to an integer; negative values count from the end.

parameters.description: Number of elements to remove from `start`.

Language core::Primitive values and coer.summary: JavaScript primitives are immutable values, while coercion converts values when an operation expects a primitive. Explicit conversion clarifies intent; == may coerce operands, whereas === does not, and Object.is() has distinct NaN and signed-zero behavior.
Language core::Primitive values and coer.explanation: JavaScript primitives are immutable values such as strings, numbers, booleans, BigInts, symbols, null, and undefined. Explicit conversions make intent clear, while == may convert operands before comparing; === compares without that conversion, and Object.is() differs for NaN and signed zero.

console.log(typeof values[0]); // "string"
console.log(Number(values[0])); // 42
console.log("42" == 42); // true: loose equality converts
console.log("42" === 42); // false: strict equality does not
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN)); // true
console.log(Object.is(-0, 0)); // false

For JavaScript APIs, inspect the relevant object for a property or method before accessing it; some features also require checking a method's return value or whether an assigned value is retained.

The `in` operator can test whether an API member is available on an object before use.
For element capabilities, create an in-memory element and inspect the relevant property.
Some detections require calling an available method and validating its specific return value.
A capability can be tested by assigning a value and checking whether the element preserves it.

Shipping JavaScript::Modules in browsers.summary: JavaScript modules are files addressed by paths or URLs and connected with import/export. Resolution is host-defined, so browser and Node package boundaries must use specifiers each runtime understands.
Shipping JavaScript::Modules in browsers.explanation: ECMAScript modules exchange values through static import and export declarations. Whether a module specifier works is decided by the host: browsers resolve URL-based paths, while Node also supports package-oriented resolution, so portable code should define clear ESM boundaries and use specifiers valid in its target runtime.

useCases.scenario: Choose relative URL paths for browser-delivered module graphs.

useCases.title: Node package integration
useCases.scenario: Use filesystem- and package-oriented resolution in Node projects.

keyPoints: Treat each module as a file addressed by a path or URL, with the exact addressing rules supplied by its host.
Use named or default exports to define a module boundary, and imports to consume the exposed bindings.
The same import text may not resolve identically in a browser and Node, so choose runtime-compatible specifiers.
Relative imports resolve from the importing module rather than from a project-wide root.
Node commonly resolves modules through its filesystem and package ecosystem, unlike browser URL loading.
Browser-oriented module graphs can use URL-based resolution, including HTTP URLs where supported.
gotchas: Do not assume that a specifier has identical resolution behavior everywhere; the host environment defines resolution.
A browser script must be marked with `type="module"` before static imports or exports can be used.
Keep browser-only globals out of modules intended to execute in Node.

Shipping JavaScript::TC39 proposal stage.summary: TC39 proposal stages describe how a JavaScript feature moves from an idea to a finished standard feature. Stage 3 recommends implementation; Stage 4 means the proposal is complete and ready for inclusion in ECMAScript.
Shipping JavaScript::TC39 proposal stage.explanation: TC39 proposals advance through stages that communicate maturity and committee expectations. Stage 3 means implementation is recommended, while Stage 4 means the feature is complete and ready for inclusion in the ECMAScript standard; earlier stages can still change or be abandoned.

keyPoints: TC39 uses Stage 0 plus maturity stages 1, 2, 2.7, 3, and 4.
A proposal advances only after committee approval for the next stage.
Stage 0 is an initial idea that is not yet being considered by the committee.
Stage 1 examines the problem, possible solutions, and cross-cutting concerns.
Stage 2 has a preferred direction, but its design may still change significantly.
Stage 3 indicates that implementations and validation should proceed.
Stage 4 marks a finished proposal suitable for inclusion in ECMAScript.

String methods::String.prototype.localeC.summary: Compares two strings according to locale-sensitive sort rules. It returns a negative, positive, or zero value based on whether the reference string comes before, after, or is equivalent to the comparison string.
String methods::String.prototype.localeC.explanation: Call the method on the string to use as the reference and pass the string to compare as the first argument. Optional locale and options arguments control language-sensitive ordering; the result is negative, positive, or zero according to their relative order. For repeated comparisons, reuse an Intl.Collator comparator.
String methods::String.prototype.localeC.syntax:
localeCompare(compareString)
localeCompare(compareString, locales)
localeCompare(compareString, locales, options)

parameters.name: compareString
parameters.description: The string to compare with the reference string; it is converted to a string if necessary.

parameters.name: locales
parameters.description: Optional BCP 47 locale tag or array of locale tags used for language-sensitive comparison.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional Intl.Collator options object controlling comparison behavior.

String methods::String.prototype.localeC.returns: An integer whose sign indicates ordering: negative if the reference string precedes compareString, positive if it follows, or 0 if they are equivalent.

Pass a locale and options to select language conventions and comparison behavior.
Interpret only the sign of the returned number: negative, positive, or zero.
Where supported, the method uses the internationalization collator machinery.
gotchas: The method only guarantees the sign of the result: negative means the reference precedes the other string, positive means it follows, and zero means equivalence.
For many comparisons, constructing one Intl.Collator and reusing its compare method can be more efficient than repeatedly calling localeCompare.

String methods::String.prototype.matchAl.summary: Returns an iterator over every match of a pattern, including capture groups and each match’s position. Use a global regular expression and consume the iterator once.

Iterating it yields exec()-shaped match arrays containing the full match, capture groups, index, input, and—when applicable—named groups. The iterator can be consumed with for...of, spread syntax, or Array.from().

parameters.description: A regular expression or an object with a Symbol.matchAll method. A non-RegExp value is converted to a global RegExp.

Each yielded match preserves numbered and named capture-group results.
Match entries follow the familiar exec() array shape.

Consume the iterator using for...of, spread syntax, or Array.from().
Arguments can customize matching by exposing Symbol.matchAll.

String methods::String.prototype.normali.summary: Converts a string to a Unicode normalization form so canonically or compatibly equivalent code-point sequences can be compared consistently. With no argument, it uses NFC.
String methods::String.prototype.normali.explanation: normalize() first converts the receiver to a string, chooses NFC when no form is supplied, and otherwise validates the requested form. It returns a normalized string using canonical or compatibility decomposition, optionally followed by composition; the original string is not changed.

parameters.description: The Unicode normalization form: "NFC", "NFD", "NFKC", or "NFKD". If omitted or undefined, "NFC" is used.

String methods::String.prototype.normali.returns: A string containing the Unicode Normalization Form of the given string.

The form parameter accepts exactly NFC, NFD, NFKC, or NFKD.
NFC decomposes canonically and then recomposes canonically.
NFKC applies compatibility decomposition and then canonical composition.

A string pattern is replaced once by replace(), while replaceAll() replaces every occurrence; regular expressions can be used, and callback replacements compute replacement text for each match.

With a string pattern, replace() changes only the first occurrence.

String methods::String.prototype.slice a.summary: slice() and substring() return a new string from a start position up to, but excluding, an end position. slice() supports negative indexes from the end; substring() clamps negative or NaN positions to zero and swaps reversed positions.
String methods::String.prototype.slice a.explanation: Both methods return a new string containing characters from a start position up to, but not including, an end position. slice() interprets negative positions from the end and returns an empty string when the normalized end is before the start; substring() clamps negative or NaN positions to zero and swaps its positions when the first exceeds the second.

console.log(text.slice(1, 4));      // "ozi"

String methods::String.prototype.split.summary: Splits a string around a separator or pattern and returns the resulting substrings in an array. An optional limit caps the number of returned entries.
String methods::String.prototype.split.explanation: `split()` searches the calling string from left to right for a separator, removes each separator match from the output, and returns the intervening substrings in an array. The separator may be a string, a regular expression, or another object implementing `Symbol.split`; an optional limit stops the result after that many entries.

The method accepts a separator and an optional limit.

String methods::String.prototype.startsW.summary: Use `startsWith()`, `endsWith()`, and `includes()` to test whether a string begins with, ends with, or contains a substring. They perform case-sensitive checks and return `true` or `false`.
String methods::String.prototype.startsW.explanation: These methods perform case-sensitive substring tests. `startsWith()` searches from a specified starting position, `endsWith()` treats its optional argument as the string’s effective end position, and `includes()` searches from an optional starting position; all return a boolean and reject regular expressions.
String methods::String.prototype.startsW.syntax:
startsWith(searchString)
startsWith(searchString, position)
endsWith(searchString)
endsWith(searchString, endPosition)
includes(searchString)
includes(searchString, position)

parameters.name: searchString
parameters.description: The string to test for at the beginning, end, or within the calling string; non-regexp values are converted to strings.

parameters.name: position / endPosition
parameters.description: For `startsWith()` and `includes()`, the search starting index; defaults to 0. For `endsWith()`, the effective end position; defaults to the string length.

String methods::String.prototype.startsW.returns: `true` when the requested characters satisfy the method's boundary or containment test, including for an empty search string; otherwise `false`.

example.title: Checking string boundaries and contents
example.code:
const value = "JavaScript runtime";

console.log(value.startsWith("Java")); // true
console.log(value.endsWith("time"));    // true
console.log(value.includes("Script"));  // true
console.log(value.includes("script"));  // false

console.log(value.startsWith("Script", 4)); // true
console.log(value.endsWith("Java", 10));    // true
console.log(value.includes("run", 10));     // true
example.explanation: The snippet checks a prefix, a suffix, and a substring, then demonstrates the optional position limits and case-sensitive matching.
